```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse=TRUE, comment="#>", fig.width=8.5,
  fig.height=5, dpi=120, out.width="100%")
library(postrank)
source(system.file("scripts", "_vignette-setup.R", package="postrank", mustWork=TRUE), local=TRUE)
analysis <- load_or_compute("case_krw_signed97")
krw <- pr_case_krw
grades <- get_grades(analysis)
profile <- get_profile(analysis)
risk <- get_risk(analysis)
ev <- analysis$fit$evaluation
n_firms <- nrow(krw$units)
grade_sizes <- table(grades)
sc <- krw$reference$single_criterion
core <- krw$reference$signed_core
scope <- krw$reference$certification_scope
fmt <- function(x, digits=3) formatC(x, digits=digits, format="f", big.mark=",")
count <- function(x) format(x, big.mark=",", scientific=FALSE, trim=TRUE)
pct <- function(x) paste0(fmt(100*x, 1), "%")
sci <- function(x) format(x, digits=3, scientific=TRUE, trim=TRUE)
firm_labels <- setNames(paste0(krw$units$firm_name, " [", krw$units$entity_id, "]"), krw$units$entity_id)
firm_labels <- vapply(firm_labels, function(z) paste(strwrap(z, width=23), collapse="\n"), "")
criterion_labels <- c(race_signed="White-name contact advantage\n(log ratio)",
  gender_signed="Male-name contact advantage\n(log ratio)")
```

Employer comparisons may concern both race and gender, with a single grade
required to summarize the two criteria. We consider such a report for the
`r n_firms` firms in the bundled Kline, Rose, and Walters case. The analysis
specifies the comparison probabilities and reporting loss, examines the
resulting disclosure and withholding, and compares the common grading with
archived single-criterion cards.

The results use a prepared analysis of the bundled input. Rendering the
article requires neither posterior model fitting nor a solver. An optional
call specifies a new analysis using HiGHS. The input and prepared result
refer to the same firms and targets, with no Gaussian approximation.

## Targets and source data {#the-question-encoded-in-the-input}

The data are adapted from Kline, Rose, and Walters' *Data and Code for: A
Discrimination Report Card*, available in the
[replication archive](https://doi.org/10.3886/E198284V1). They concern the
original correspondence experiment. A grade here describes the modelled
contact differences in those data; it is not a statement about an employer's
current practices or the effect of an intervention.

```{r input}
library(postrank)
krw <- pr_case_krw
dim(krw$input$e)
krw$input$targets
```

The first target is the signed white-name contact advantage,
\(\log(p_{white})-\log(p_{black})\). The second is the signed male-name contact
advantage, \(\log(p_{male})-\log(p_{female})\). Larger values receive higher
reporting priority on each criterion. Consequently, grade 1 denotes the
higher-priority group. A negative gender target means a female-name contact
advantage; taking its absolute value would answer a different question.

Both targets are log ratios. Their posterior means differ from the
logarithms of posterior mean probability ratios, and exponentiating a
posterior mean log ratio generally differs from taking the posterior mean
ratio. Retaining the supplied scale ensures a common interpretation of the
target, intervals and pairwise comparisons.

The source README states, “The data are licensed under a Creative
Commons/CC-BY-NC license.” Its license version is unspecified. The bundled
adaptation retains the same noncommercial source notice. See
`?pr_case_krw` for attribution and the extraction description. The package
code license does not replace those conditions.

### Posterior specification {#what-distribution-do-these-numbers-describe}

The original empirical-Bayes analysis supplies posterior grids. This case
uses continuous uniform cells whose boundaries lie between retained grid
midpoints, preserving each cell's posterior mass. The first race cell has
nonnegative support. The fitted prior and its parameters remain fixed. The
supplied means and `r count(100*krw$input$summaries$level)`% equal-tail marginal
intervals describe those same continuous cells.

For distinct firms, `e[i, j, k]` is the posterior probability that firm
`i`'s target is no larger than firm `j`'s target on criterion `k`. It is
therefore the expected directional error when the report places `i` above
`j`. These probabilities were calculated assuming conditional independence
of firms given the fixed empirical-Bayes quantities. Importing the array
preserves this assumption without establishing its empirical validity.

The archive's `Pi` matrix, discrete grid atoms and the continuous cell law
used here represent different probability specifications. `Pi` is a
published comparison reference with its own conventions. Grid atoms assign
mass to nodes and can produce positive equality probabilities; the continuous
law distributes each mass over an interval and declares zero equality
probability for distinct firms. The archive's plotting repair and the grade
generator's probability floor are not applied to this input. Their reference
records are retained separately in `krw$reference$archive_pi`.

Criterion-wise probabilities and marginal summaries suffice for the
weighted loss below, which adds expected errors across criteria. The input
contains neither target draws nor a within-firm joint distribution of race
and gender. Consequently, it does not identify probabilities involving a
composite race-and-gender target or simultaneous dominance on both criteria.

## Loss and grade constraints {#choose-the-comparisons-worth-reporting}

The reporting loss assigns equal criterion weights, a withholding cost of
`r fmt(analysis$settings$tau, 2)`, and at most
`r analysis$settings$G_max` grades. The weights average expected directional
errors; they neither combine the posterior means nor impose equal precision
across criteria.

```{r policy}
settings <- postrank_settings(
  weights = c(race_signed = .5, gender_signed = .5),
  tau = .25,
  G_max = 4L
)
```

There are \(M=\binom{n}{2}\) unordered firm pairs. A grade either discloses a
direction for a pair or leaves it unordered. Let \(N\) be the number disclosed
and \(E_k\) the expected number of wrong-direction disclosures on criterion
\(k\). The risk for this policy is

\[
 R(g)=\frac{\sum_k w_k E_k(g)+\tau\{M-N(g)\}}{M}.
\]

Each pair receives a common grade relation whose expected error may differ
across criteria. Assigning all firms to one grade is admissible and gives
risk \(\tau\) by withholding every comparison. This action makes no equality
claim about firms. Likewise, an increase in the grade cap expands the
permitted number of groups without requiring all grades to be occupied.

The following optional call uses the supplied interval level, explicitly
selects a solver and imposes a time limit. It is not executed during document
rendering. For a new run, the returned status and bound determine whether
optimality was established within tolerance; the time limit alone provides
no such assurance.

```{r optional-fresh-analysis, eval=FALSE}
analysis <- postrank(
  krw$input, settings = settings,
  level = krw$input$summaries$level,
  backend = "highs",
  control = postrank_control(time_limit = 30, threads = 1L, seed = 1304L),
  fragility = FALSE
)
```

## Common grading {#what-the-common-grade-discloses}

```{r result}
analysis
get_risk(analysis)
```

The prepared result has `r length(grade_sizes)` grades containing
`r paste(as.integer(grade_sizes), collapse=" / ")` firms. It discloses
`r count(ev$N)` of `r count(ev$M)` pairs (`r pct(ev$N/ev$M)`) and withholds
`r count(ev$M-ev$N)`. Its risk is `r fmt(risk$risk, 11)`, compared with
`r fmt(analysis$settings$tau, 2)` for withholding all pairs under the same
settings. The large middle grade thus reflects substantial withholding at
the specified cost.

The returned status is `r risk$status`, meaning optimal within the numerical
solver tolerances for the supplied coefficient problem. The recorded gap is
`r risk$gap`. The result also retains a warning: the reported lower bound
exceeded the validated action risk by `r sci(analysis$fit$objective$risk_bound_minus_action_risk)`,
within its bound-validation tolerance of
`r sci(analysis$fit$objective$bound_validation_risk_tolerance)`, and was clamped
to the action risk. Thus a displayed zero gap is a numerical optimization
statement conditional on this finite probability table. It does not certify
the underlying posterior approximation, the empirical-Bayes assumptions, or
the firms' true contact differences.

```{r criterion-results}
profile <- get_profile(analysis)
knitr::kable(profile[, c("criterion", "weight", "E", "E_over_N", "E_over_M", "risk")],
  digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
```

The expected error per disclosed pair is
`r fmt(profile$E_over_N[profile$criterion=="race_signed"], 3)` for race and
`r fmt(profile$E_over_N[profile$criterion=="gender_signed"], 3)` for gender.
These ratios use the same `r count(ev$N)` disclosed pairs. By contrast,
`E_over_M` divides by all `r count(ev$M)` pairs. Neither quantity is a count
of observed mistakes: both average over the declared posterior uncertainty.
The criterion risks also include the cost of the withheld pairs.

```{r criterion-profile, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Expected wrong-direction comparisons per disclosed pair. Both criteria describe the same common grade, and both use N as the denominator."}
postrank_plot_profile(analysis, show = "E_over_N")
```

A weighted loss may retain a direction with greater uncertainty on one
criterion when the other criterion provides sufficient support. Equal
weights can therefore yield different criterion-specific errors. This
analysis imposes no separate criterion error budget, so `q` is unavailable
in the extracted profile rather than equal to zero.

## Posterior summaries for selected firms {#read-a-named-report-without-hiding-the-withheld-group}

The following report card includes every firm outside the largest grade
and a spaced selection within that grade. This display allocation retains
the small outer groups and permits legible intervals. It changes neither
the grading nor the population represented by the full result, and is not a
representative subsample. All `r n_firms` firms remain available in
`as.data.frame(analysis)`.

```{r select-firms}
grades <- get_grades(analysis)
largest_grade <- as.integer(names(which.max(table(grades))))
middle_ids <- names(grades)[grades == largest_grade]
selected <- c(
  names(grades)[grades != largest_grade],
  middle_ids[round(seq(1, length(middle_ids), length.out = 5))]
)
firm_labels <- setNames(
  paste0(krw$units$firm_name, " [", krw$units$entity_id, "]"),
  krw$units$entity_id
)
firm_labels <- vapply(firm_labels, function(z)
  paste(strwrap(z, width = 23), collapse = "\n"), "")
```

```{r named-card, fig.height=8.5, fig.cap=paste0("Selected firms, with identifiers retained beside their names. Points and intervals are marginal means and ", format(100*krw$input$summaries$level), "% equal-tail intervals from the continuous cell law. The original common grades are unchanged.")}
postrank_plot_report_card(
  analysis, entities = selected, entity_labels = firm_labels,
  criterion_labels = c(
    race_signed = "White-name contact advantage\n(log ratio)",
    gender_signed = "Male-name contact advantage\n(log ratio)"
  ), ncol = 2
)
```

The horizontal intervals describe uncertainty about firm targets, whereas
the grades specify the reporting action across firms. The grading is chosen
from pairwise directional probabilities and the declared loss, rather than
interval overlap. Firms assigned to the same grade may therefore have
different posterior means, intervals and targets.

Firm names provide display labels, while IDs retain the correspondence with
source rows. The estimates and standard errors in `krw$units` are source
estimates and differ from the posterior summaries shown here. The latter
are available in `as.data.frame(analysis, what = "report_card")`.
Combining source standard errors with posterior means would not reconstruct
the reported intervals.

## Evaluation of archived cards under a common loss {#put-the-archived-cards-on-the-same-loss-before-comparing}

The archived single-criterion cards use
\(\lambda\) = `r fmt(sc$lambda, 2)`, corresponding to
\(\tau=\lambda/(1+\lambda)\) = `r fmt(sc$tau, 2)`. The common analysis above
uses \(\tau\) = `r fmt(analysis$settings$tau, 2)`. Numerically equal lambda and
tau values therefore do not denote the same withholding cost. The original
single-criterion cards also permit up to `r sc$G_max` grades and address one
target at a time. Direct comparison of their original losses with the common
loss would therefore compare values of different objective functions.

For a common comparison, each archived card can be evaluated under the
current signed cell probabilities, equal criterion weights and common
withholding cost. Supplying its named grade vector to `postrank_compare()`
performs this fixed-action evaluation. The archived optimization is neither
rerun nor assigned a new optimization status.

```{r compare-actions}
comparison <- postrank_compare(
  analysis,
  archived_common = krw$reference$signed_core$grade,
  published_race = krw$reference$single_criterion$grade$race,
  published_gender = krw$reference$single_criterion$grade$gender,
  baselines = character()
)
knitr::kable(comparison$table[, c("method", "risk", "N", "G", "status", "family_feasible")],
  digits = 6, row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r compare-figure, fig.height=5.5, fig.cap="All displayed risks use the current signed cell input and one common policy. Supplied archived actions are evaluated only; their original numerical statuses are not inherited."}
postrank_plot_compare(comparison)
```

The archived and prepared common actions differ in
`r count(sum(comparison$relations[comparison$relations$method=="archived_common", c("n_new_disclosed","n_new_withheld","n_reversed")]))`
pair relations. The archived race and gender cards disclose
`r count(sc$cell_metrics$race$N)` and `r count(sc$cell_metrics$gender$N)`
pairs, respectively. These evaluations describe the trade-off between
disclosure and expected error for the fixed actions under the common loss;
they do not establish a general advantage over single-criterion reports.

Even for a fixed action, its evaluated risk depends on the coefficient law.
For the archived common action, the archive-reference risk is
`r fmt(core$archive_metrics$risk, 11)` and the continuous-cell risk is
`r fmt(core$cell_metrics$risk, 11)`, a difference of
`r sci(core$cell_metrics$risk-core$archive_metrics$risk)`.
The difference results from the probability reference rather than a new
optimization. Its magnitude is retained when assessing numerical
reproduction.

## Changes of target and the limits of the stored evidence

The inputs `krw$alternatives$race` and `krw$alternatives$gender` support
single-criterion analyses of the same signed targets.
`krw$alternatives$absolute_gender` retains signed race and replaces gender
by the magnitude of its contact gap. This input folds the original
continuous cells, including those crossing zero, and provides the
corresponding probabilities and summaries.

Absolute gender assigns high priority to a large advantage in either
direction. It therefore changes the target even when the numerical policy
settings are held fixed. The stored action is a separate reference whose
risk cannot be interpreted as an improvement over the signed analysis.
Changes in weights or tau likewise require evaluation or optimization under
the newly specified loss.

The source research campaign completed
`r scope$solver_and_coefficient_gate_passed + scope$validated_independent_reference`
of `r scope$total_unique_problems` distinct numerical problems:
`r scope$solver_and_coefficient_gate_passed` passed its solver and
finite-reference coefficient checks, and
`r scope$validated_independent_reference` had an independent reference
validation. The other `r scope$not_run` were not run. Those qualifications
belong to their declared research calculations. They are neither a completed
sensitivity sweep nor additional certification of this prepared package
result. This article does not run a weight path, refit the prior, or fill in
the missing research problems.
